381.event: In 1905 the Sanskrit scholar Rudrapatna Shamasastry, working as a librarian at the Oriental Library in Mysore, identified a manuscript of the Arthashastra, the ancient Indian treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya, which had been known only through later references and was thought to be lost. He published the Sanskrit text in 1909 and an English translation in 1915. The publication brought the treatise to the attention of scholars around the world.
381.explanation: The rediscovery gave historians a detailed ancient Indian account of how a state should be built and run, including its army, revenue, ministers, alliances and fortifications. It transformed the study of early Indian political thought.
381.tie_back: The kural lists the parts a ruler must possess, army, people, resources, ministers, allies and forts, and the rediscovered Arthashastra is the classic Indian treatise that analyses the state through closely similar elements.
381._accuracy_note: Next-best: the event recovers a text that sets out the same theory of the state's limbs, but it is a scholarly discovery rather than a ruler who actually possessed all six and stood like a lion among kings.

382.event_title: Elizabeth I addresses her troops at Tilbury
382.event: As the Spanish Armada threatened England in the summer of 1588, Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, commander of the land forces, arranged for Queen Elizabeth I to visit the army camp at Tilbury on the Thames. In early August she reviewed the troops and delivered a speech meant to encourage the men to stand firm against a possible invasion led by the Duke of Parma. The speech became one of the most celebrated in English history.
382.explanation: At a moment of national danger the queen went in person among her soldiers rather than remaining safe in London. Her visit became a lasting symbol of a ruler's courage and energy in a crisis.
382.tie_back: Valluvar names fearlessness and energetic drive among the qualities a ruler must never lack, and Elizabeth showed both by going to the front to rally her army.
382._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the event shows courage and energy, but not the generosity and wisdom the kural also lists, and the kural stresses never lacking them rather than one display.

383.event_title: Peter the Great works in foreign shipyards during the Grand Embassy
383.place: Zaandam and Amsterdam, Dutch Republic; Deptford, England
383.event: In 1697 Tsar Peter I of Russia travelled west with a large diplomatic mission, the Grand Embassy, under the assumed name of Pyotr Mikhailov. In the Dutch Republic he studied shipbuilding and worked as a ship's carpenter in the Dutch East India Company's yard, and in England he worked at the Royal Navy dockyard at Deptford and visited factories, arsenals and other institutions. On his return he began sweeping reforms and built up a Russian navy.
383.explanation: Peter combined a tireless drive to act with a determination to learn practical skills himself, and then had the resolve to impose far-reaching changes on his country.
383.tie_back: The kural says a ruler must never lose alertness, learning and firm resolve, and Peter's hands-on study abroad followed by bold reform displays all three.
383._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the triad of vigilance, learning and resolve in a ruler, though Peter's reign also included harsh methods the kural would not endorse.

384.event_title: King Haakon VII refuses to appoint Quisling
384.event: After Germany invaded Norway, the German envoy Curt Brauer met King Haakon VII on 10 April 1940 and demanded that he dismiss the lawful government and appoint a government headed by the collaborator Vidkun Quisling. At an extraordinary Council of State the king said he could not comply and would rather abdicate than appoint Quisling, while leaving the decision to his ministers, who supported him. German aircraft then bombed Nybergsund, and the king later continued the resistance from exile in Britain.
384.explanation: Haakon refused to lend royal authority to an illegitimate regime even under direct military threat. His refusal became a rallying point for Norwegian resistance throughout the occupation.
384.tie_back: The kural describes a king who never swerves from righteousness, removes what is wrong and never loses courage or honour, and Haakon's refusal joined justice and courage at the cost of great personal danger.
384._accuracy_note: A very close illustration of righteousness and courage held together under pressure, although the 'removing wrongdoing from the land' element was achieved only later with the Allies.

385.event_title: The Inca state's network of storehouses
385.event: The Inca Empire built large numbers of state storehouses, called qollqa or colcas, along its road network and near administrative centres. Surplus food, cloth, raw materials and other goods produced through labour owed to the state were stored in them and recorded by officials using knotted-string quipu. The stores supplied armies and state workers and were used to support communities when harvests failed.
385.explanation: The storehouse system turned the empire's production into a reserve that could be protected and redistributed where it was needed. It helped the empire survive poor harvests and sustain its armies across great distances.
385.tie_back: Valluvar describes good government as creating wealth, collecting it, guarding it and distributing it wisely, and the Inca storehouses carried out each of these four tasks.
385._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the four-step cycle of public wealth, though it describes a long-running institution rather than a single dated event.

386.event_title: King Christian X's daily rides through occupied Copenhagen
386.event: During the German occupation of Denmark, King Christian X rode on horseback through the streets of Copenhagen every day, where citizens could see and greet him. The rides became a public sign that he had not abandoned his claim to Danish sovereignty and won him great popular support. Later legends, such as the story that he wore a yellow star, are not true, but the daily rides are well documented.
386.explanation: By making himself visible and approachable to ordinary people at a time of national humiliation, the king strengthened the morale and unity of the country.
386.tie_back: The kural praises a king who is easy for his people to see and approach, and Christian X's daily appearance among Copenhagen's citizens made the whole land admired for its quiet steadfastness.
386._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a ruler being easily seen by his people, though the sources say little about his manner of speech, the kural's second condition.

387.event_title: The Jam Sahib of Nawanagar shelters Polish refugee children
387.event: During the Second World War, Polish children, many of them orphans, who had been released from the Soviet Union with nowhere to go were brought to India. Maharaja Digvijaysinhji, the Jam Sahib of Nawanagar, set up a camp for them near his summer palace at Balachadi from 1942 and maintained it largely at his own expense, with a school, a Polish library and activities that kept their culture alive. Hundreds of children lived under his protection until the camp closed and they were moved on after the war, and he is remembered in Poland as the Good Maharaja.
387.explanation: The maharaja's generosity was matched by personal warmth toward children far from home, and his care earned lasting gratitude between two distant nations.
387.tie_back: The kural says the world follows a ruler who gives with kind words and protects those who come to him, and the Jam Sahib gave refuge and care to children who had lost everything.
387._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of a ruler who gives, protects those who come to him and wins lasting affection, though the kural's political reward of the world following his word is only loosely matched.

388.event: Augustus, the first Roman emperor, died on 19 August 14 CE, and on 17 September the Senate enrolled him among the gods of the Roman state with the title divus, the deified one. Ancient accounts credit the honour to his achievements, including restoring peace after decades of civil war and maintaining law and order. A temple to the Divine Augustus was built in Rome, and the deification set a precedent for later emperors.
388.explanation: Augustus had resisted being named a god while alive, but after his death the state honoured the ruler who had brought order and security as divine. His case shows how rulers who were seen to protect their people could be raised to sacred status.
388.tie_back: The kural says the king who rules justly and protects his people will be regarded as a god, and Rome formally deified Augustus for bringing peace and order.
388._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of conditional deification earned by protection and order, though the deification was also an act of state policy and Augustus's rise involved civil war.

389.event_title: Frederick Douglass confronts Abraham Lincoln about Black soldiers
389.place: The White House, Washington, D.C., United States
389.event: The abolitionist Frederick Douglass, who had been recruiting Black soldiers for the Union Army, went to the White House on 10 August 1863 and told President Lincoln he could no longer recruit because Black soldiers received less pay than white soldiers, had no chance of promotion and were not protected when captured. Lincoln received him, listened seriously and explained his reasons, and Douglass later recalled that the president was serious and even troubled by what he had said. Although not all his demands were met, Douglass came away with lasting respect for Lincoln's openness.
389.explanation: A president in the middle of a civil war gave his full attention to blunt criticism from a man born into slavery, and the meeting began a relationship of mutual respect.
389.tie_back: The kural praises a ruler gracious enough to bear words that are bitter to hear, and Lincoln received Douglass's sharp complaints with patience and seriousness.
389._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a leader patiently hearing bitter criticism, though the kural's promise of the whole world sheltering under such a ruler goes beyond what one meeting shows.

390.event_title: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet for his people
390.event: King Sejong, the fourth ruler of Korea's Joseon dynasty, oversaw the creation of a new phonetic alphabet, completed around 1443, so that ordinary people who could not master Chinese characters could learn to read and write. In 1446 he promulgated it as Hunminjeongeum, the Proper Sounds to Instruct the People, with an explanatory text. That 1446 text is now inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, and the alphabet, Hangul, is used throughout Korea today.
390.explanation: Sejong used royal power not to glorify himself but to give literacy to common people, and his reign is remembered as a golden age of Korean culture and science.
390.tie_back: The kural crowns as the light among kings the ruler who combines generosity, compassion, just rule and care for his people, and Sejong's alphabet was a gift of care to all his subjects.
390._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a ruler whose care for ordinary people became his lasting light, though the event centres on one achievement rather than all four qualities together.
